title: Spring 2025 Midterm II
notes: Students could bring one handwritten sheet of notes. The exam has 15 pages plus appendices: Gctx interface, Widget interface, notifier implementation and Java String docs.

items.prompt: The pictured almost-queue q1 has a single node (v = 1) whose next field points back to itself, with head and tail both pointing to that node. Which part of the queue invariant does it break: (1), (2a), (2b), or is it valid?
items.code:
type 'a qnode = { v : 'a; mutable next : 'a qnode option }
type 'a queue = { mutable head : 'a qnode option; mutable tail : 'a qnode option }

Invariant:
(1) head and tail are both None or both Some
(2) if head = Some h and tail = Some t:
  (2a) t is reachable from h by following next pointers
  (2b) t.next = None
items.notes: head and tail are both Some node1, so (1) and (2a) hold. node1.next = Some node1, not None, so (2b) fails.

items.prompt: Write make_q1 () so that let q1 = make_q1 () produces the pictured almost-queue q1: one node with v = 1 whose next points to itself, and head and tail both pointing to that node.
Fill in the expected result of contains_qn qn1 [qn2; qn3], where qn2 is bound to the same node as qn1 and contains_qn uses physical equality (==).
items.code:
let rec contains_qn (e : 'a qnode) (l : 'a qnode list) : bool =
  begin match l with
  | [] -> false
  | hd :: tl -> if e == hd then true else contains_qn e tl
  end

let test () : bool =
  let qn1 = { v = 1 ; next = None } in
  let qn2 = qn1 in
  let qn3 = { v = 3 ; next = Some qn1 } in
  contains_qn qn1 [ qn2 ; qn3 ] = ____
items.notes: qn2 is an alias for qn1 (same heap node), so qn1 == qn2 holds on the first list element.

items.prompt: Is the given mystery function on bool queues tail recursive? (You don't need to work out what it computes.)
items.code:
let mystery (q : bool queue) : bool =
  let rec loop (qno : bool qnode option) : bool =
    begin match qno with
    | None -> true
    | Some qn -> loop qn.next && qn.v
    end in
  loop q.head
items.notes: Function application binds tighter than &&, so the body is (loop qn.next) && qn.v; qn.v must still be checked after the call returns.

items.prompt: Complete remove_cycle, which truncates an almost-queue so that the first node referring to itself or to an earlier node becomes the last node. A valid queue must be left unchanged. Fill in the Some next_qn branch and the final call to loop. You may use contains_qn but no other library functions.
items.code:
type 'a qnode = { v : 'a; mutable next : 'a qnode option }
type 'a queue = { mutable head : 'a qnode option; mutable tail : 'a qnode option }

let rec contains_qn (e : 'a qnode) (l : 'a qnode list) : bool =
  begin match l with
  | [] -> false
  | hd :: tl -> if e == hd then true else contains_qn e tl
  end

let remove_cycle (q: 'a queue) : unit =
  let rec loop (qno : 'a qnode option) (l: 'a qnode list) : unit =
    begin match qno with
    | None -> ()
    | Some qn ->
      begin match qn.next with
      | None -> ()
      | Some next_qn -> ____
      end
    end in
  loop ____
items.key:
let remove_cycle (q : 'a queue) : unit =
  let rec loop (qno : 'a qnode option) (l : 'a qnode list) : unit =
    begin match qno with
    | None -> ()
    | Some qn ->
      begin match qn.next with
      | None -> ()
      | Some next_qn ->
        if contains_qn next_qn l then
          (qn.next <- None; q.tail <- Some qn)
        else loop qn.next (qn :: l)
      end
    end
  in loop q.head []
items.notes: Checking contains_qn next_qn (qn :: l) instead also works and catches a self-loop one step sooner. Setting q.tail is required so tail ends up on the new last node.

items.prompt: Using the notifier implementation in Appendix C, give the type of the anonymous function on lines 12 to 14 (the handle function).
When the anonymous function on lines 12 to 14 is allocated as a closure in the heap, which stack bindings must it copy? Options: w, listeners, contents, List.iter, g, e.
items.key: w, listeners (not contents, not List.iter, not g/e)
items.notes: g and e are the function's own parameters. contents is a record field, not a binding. List.iter is a top-level library function.

items.prompt: Implement clock init, which returns a clock widget, its notifier controller, and an int value controller for the time. Draw a circular clock face centered in a 400x400 canvas plus a hand from the center to find_endpoint of the current time. Fill in the repaint body, the canvas call and the return value.
items.notes: The prompt says '150 x 150 ellipse', but r = 150 is passed as the radius, which matches find_endpoint's radius-150 circle.

items.prompt: Given a clock (starting at 12) next to a label reading "Zzzzz", use the clock's value controller vc so that the label changes to "Wake up" when the time reaches 5.
items.code:
let clock_w, nc, vc = clock 12
let label_w, lc = label "Zzzzz"
let top = hpair clock_w (hpair (space (10,10)) label_w)
(* add your code here *)
items.key:
vc.add_change_listener (fun x ->
  if x = 5 then lc.set_label "Wake up")
items.notes: The official solution writes lc.set_text, but the label_controller field in the appendix is set_label.

items.prompt: What happens when this code runs? Options: s.length returns 0; s.length is skipped; NullPointerException; does not compile; none of the above.
What does this code print? Options: true; false; null; does not compile; none of the above.
What does this code print when comparing two char arrays with ==? Options: true; false; null; does not compile; none of the above.
items.notes: toCharArray returns a new array, and == on arrays compares references.

items.prompt: What happens when this code runs? Options: prints "OCaml"; prints 2; prints null; ArrayIndexOutOfBoundsException; none of the above.
Which of these declarations validly create a Java array holding "1", "2" and "3"? Select all that apply, or none of the above.
items.key: String[] arr = {"1", "2", "3"}; and String[] arr = { new String("1"), new String("2"), new String("3")}; (the first and fourth options).
items.notes: new String(new char[]{...}) makes a String, not an array. new int[]{1, 2, 3} can't be assigned to String[], so it doesn't compile.

items.prompt: Fill in the expected value for a test that requests a zero-by-zero rectangle from a non-null jagged input. It should be a 0x0 2D array.
Choose an input for which extractRectangle(0, 0, input) should return null.

Implement extractRectangle(h, w, input), which copies the h x w rectangle from the upper-left corner of a possibly jagged input. Return null if any part of the input is null, h or w is negative, or there aren't enough values. It must never throw ArrayIndexOutOfBounds or NullPointerException; return null instead.
items.notes: The printed exam headed this part removeRectangle, with a fill-in skeleton that walks every row. The official solution ignores that skeleton and writes extractRectangle from scratch, so that is the key. Note the last loop: 'any part of the input is null' includes rows below the rectangle.
